3)  Preamble 

Marine Insurance is a type of insurance that provides coverage for various risks associated with 
maritime activities, specifically the transportation of goods, cargo, and vessels across waterways. 
It  is  designed  to  protect  the  interests  of  the  parties  involved  in  maritime  trade,  including  ship 
owners, cargo owners, and other entities operating in the maritime industry. 

The  main  purpose  of  Marine  Insurance,  also  referred  to  as  Maritime  Insurance,  is  to  mitigate 
financial losses arising from perils and hazards that can happen during sea voyages or while goods 
are in transit over water. 

Maritime Insurance typically covers a range of risks, including:  

▪  Cargo Insurance – it provides coverage for the goods being transported, compensating the 

cargo owner for losses or damages incurred during transit.

The General Consumption Tax: Treatment of Insurance coverages for marine activities, 
aviation and other related activities carried on at a shipping port and international airport 
in Jamaica. 

▪  Liability Insurance – it offers protection against liabilities arising from third party claims, 
such as collisions, property damage, pollution, or injuries caused by the insured vessel. 

▪  Freight Insurance – this covers the loss of freight revenue that a ship owner may suffer due 

to damage to the cargo or vessel, resulting in the inability to deliver the goods. 

▪  Hull & Machine Insurance – this type of coverage protects the ship owner against damage 

to the vessel itself, including its hull, machinery and equipment. 

▪  War Risk Insurance – Coverage for protection from potential losses caused by war-related 

events.  

Marine Insurance policies can be tailored to the specific needs of the insured parties and can vary 
based on the type of cargo, route, duration of the voyage, etc. They may provide coverage for a 
single voyage or be issued as an annual policy to cover multiple shipments or vessels. 

Aviation Insurance 

According to OECD’s publication2, this is a type of insurance where “insurers provide insurance 
cover  for  insureds  (airlines,  manufacturers,  airports,  service  providers  {refuellers,  caterers, 
security screeners and the like}) against loss, damage and liability”.   

The principal insurance coverages, all of which exclude war risks (through an exclusion clause), 
are:  

▪  Hull – damage to the aircraft itself.  

▪  Passenger – liability for death or injury 

▪  Third  party  –  liability  for  death  and  bodily  injury  (BI)  caused  by  aircraft  accidents  and 

property damage (PD) external to the aircraft.  

▪  Airport Operators Liability - Airport operations liability insurance covers the liability of 
entities  which  operate  and  provide  facilities  at  airports,  including  airport  owners  and 
operators,  hangar  keepers  ,  air  traffic  control  services,  maintenance,  repair  and  service 
facilities, aircraft refuellers and flying clubs and schools 3

 TECHNICAL ADVISORY 
The General Consumption Tax: Treatment of Insurance coverages for marine activities, 
aviation and other related activities carried on at a shipping port and international airport 
in Jamaica. 

▪  Airport Premises  Liability  - covers the liability of an owner or lessee of premises at  an 
airport for loss, damage or injury occurring on the premises, usually because of the owner’s 
or lessee’s fault4.  

▪  Ground  Handlers  Liability  - coverage  in  respect  of  the  risks  associated  with  the  airside 
handling of the aircraft including ramp turn-around, baggage handling, aircraft cleaning 
and aircraft marshalling. 

Aviation War risks coverages (“war, hijacking and other perils” including terrorism) are: 

▪  Hull –insured in a separate war risk insurance market.  

▪  Passenger and third party – added to the principal liability policies by an extension 

standard insurance clause known as AVN52.  

Aviation war risk insurance provides coverage for hostile acts of violence against airlines, such as 
terrorism, hijackings, and sabotage. These cover for each and every occurrence for the insured 
party. Due to the unprecedented extent of exposure revealed on September 11, 2001, commercial 
insurance  cover  for  passenger  and  third  party  war  risks  were  revised  for  both  the  cost  and  the 
increased  risks.  It  has  since  been  offered  as  a  separate  aviation  policy  as  it  is  excluded  from 
standard insurance policies due to the high risks involved. 

4)  Purpose of this Technical Advisory 

The purpose of this Technical Advisory is to provide guidance on the GCT treatment for Marine, 
Aviation and other related insurance coverages within the context of the various activities carried 
on at a port and international airport in Jamaica. In particular, it aims to clarify how the General 
Consumption Tax (GCT) exemption in Item 27 of Part II of the Third Schedule, applies to the 
insurance policies that provide coverage for the exempt services mentioned in that provision. It will 
therefore explain the implications and practical application of this exemption to such insurance 
policies.

8)  Background 

Goods and services specified in the Third Schedule are classified as exempt from GCT. Services 
that fall in the exempt category include “Services (excluding catering services) rendered at a port 
or international airport in Jamaica in connection with the importation or exportation of goods or 
the transportation of people into or out of Jamaica”. 

Where a service is exempt from the tax, no GCT is charged on the supply of such service. This 
also means that an input tax credit is not allowed for the GCT paid on the inputs used to make 
these supplies because they are non-taxable. Instead, the GCT paid is to be included as part of the 
cost of those goods and services.

The General Consumption Tax: Treatment of Insurance coverages for marine activities,

9)  The Issue 

Registered  taxpayers  in  the  Shipping/Marine,  Aviation  and  Insurance  Industry,  particularly 
insurance brokers, are unsettled about: 

▪  Whether Marine Insurance and Aviation Insurance qualify as services rendered at a port or 
airport ‘in connection with’ the importation or exportation of goods or transportation of 
people into or out of Jamaica, and  

▪  Whether these services fall within the ambit of services that are exempt from GCT under 

the Third Schedule of the Act. 

Varied interpretations have been applied when determining whether a service is rendered at a port 
or international airport in Jamaica ‘in connection with’ the importation or exportation of goods or 
the transportation of people into or out of the island. However, in this Technical Advisory, that 
determination will be made by addressing the following questions: 

(1) Does  the  service  have  to  be  executed  directly  at  the  location  of  a  shipping  port  or 

international airport in Jamaica? 

(2) How does one determine that a service is ‘in connection with’ an activity?  

(3) Does  Marine/  Maritime,  Aviation  or  other  related  insurance  services  qualify  for 

exemption pursuant to the Third Schedule of the GCT Act? 

10) TAJ’s Position 

•  Marine Insurance and Aviation Insurance are typically regarded as financial services that 
require no physical presence or activity at a port or international airport.  These services 
are not inextricably linked to the actual movement or handling of goods or people at the 
port or international airport. It should be noted that maritime or marine insurance services 
or aviation insurance services cover a broad range of risks including: 

▪  Storms and natural disasters 
▪  Fire and explosion 
▪  Piracy and theft 
▪  Collision and grounding 
▪ 

Jettison (throwing cargo overboard to save the ship) 

Advisory #: 022026/01/GCT-TA 
DISCLAIMER: This Advisory is a guide only and is not a substitute for the General Consumption Tax 
(GCT), GCT Regulations or any other relevant Legislation.   

6 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 TECHNICAL ADVISORY 
The General Consumption Tax: Treatment of Insurance coverages for marine activities, 
aviation and other related activities carried on at a shipping port and international airport 
in Jamaica. 

▪  General average (shared loss among stakeholders) 

•  The cost of the marine and aviation insurance is directly related to all of the risks covered, 
which means the risks associated with the losses that may occur at the port or airport cannot 
be seen as the main or dominant risk of a policy. Therefore, the majority of the premium 
costs is not associated with any activity at the port. The distinctive nature of this insurance 
is  that  it  provides  protection  against  financial  loss  in  relation  to  shipping  and  logistics, 
which  may  or  may  not  occur  at  a  port.  Marine  and  Aviation  insurance  is  a  financial 
contingency tool that:  
▪  Transfers Risk; 
▪  Provides Liquidity; 
▪  Supports Continuity; 
▪  Provides predictability.  

•  Given the nature and purpose of Marine and Aviation Insurance, it can be concluded that 
they do not fall within the scope of the exempted activities provided for in Item 27 of Part 
II of the Third Schedule. For these services to fall within the construct of this particular 
provision of the GCT Act, they must satisfy the following two conditions: 
1.  They must be location-specific services that can only be physically rendered at a 

port or international airport; and 

2.  They  must  be  services  that  have  a  direct  or  immediate  link  to  the  importation  or 

exportation of goods or the transportation of people into and out of Jamaica. 

The construction of Item 27 using the terms “rendered at” and “in connection with” implies 
operational type of services inextricably linked to the importation or exportation of goods or 
the transportation of people. Item 27 did not contemplate remote financial services that cover 
contingencies that may never materialize.  

• 

It is TAJ’s view, that for services to be deemed to be “in connection with…” as per Item 
27  in  Part  II  of  the  Third  Schedule  to  the  GCT  Act,  they  must  be  sufficiently,  closely 
connected with the importation and exportation of goods or the transportation of people 
into and out of Jamaica. In other words, they must be highly essential or integral to the 
movement of goods or people into or out of the island. 

•  Some of the operational services that meet both conditions include, for example:  

▪  Cargo handling and storage  
▪  Freight forwarding 

Advisory #: 022026/01/GCT-TA

 TECHNICAL ADVISORY 
The General Consumption Tax: Treatment of Insurance coverages for marine activities, 
aviation and other related activities carried on at a shipping port and international airport 
in Jamaica. 

▪  Security services specifically rendered at the port 
▪  Maintenance and repair of transportation equipment specifically used at the port 

or airport 

▪  Passenger handling  
▪  Baggage handling  
▪  Air traffic control  
▪  Port management  
▪  Marine pilotage or docking Aircraft ground handling 

•  As a consequence of the foregoing, insurance products such as Air Cargo Policy, Aviation 
Liability Policy, Aviation War Risk Policy, Transport Insurance or any classification of 
insurance  which  is    used  to  provide  coverage  for  activities  associated  with  the  actual 
movement or handling of goods or people at a port or international airport into and out of 
Jamaica, do not fall within the ambit of the GCT exemption provision. In addition, these 
particular types of insurance can be properly classified as  'financial services'. However, 
they do not qualify for exemption under Item 23 (which extensively classifies the 'financial 
services' that qualify), nor under any other Item in Part II of the Third Schedule."  

•  Finally, the position of TAJ on the above issues is not a new interpretation of the legislation 
and therefore remains consistent and unchanged. The Advisory merely serves to provide 
clarity and further reinforcement of the operation of the law as it relates to how the above 
activities/services shall be treated for the purposes of GCT.  

11) 

Analysis of the Issues 

Issue #1: Does the service have to be executed directly at the location of a port or 
international airport in Jamaica? 

Meaning of the phrase “rendered at the port or international airport” 

•  The meaning of the phrase ‘rendered at the port or international airport’ is of importance 
in the interpretation of Item 27 of Part II of the Third Schedule. According to Black’s Law 
Dictionary,  the  word  ‘rendered’  is  a  term  that  means  inter  alia  “to  perform  a  service”, 
Likewise, the Merriam-Webster Dictionary defines the word to mean, “to do (a service) 
for another”.   

Advisory #: 022026/01/GCT-TA 
DISCLAIMER: This Advisory is a guide only and is not a substitute for the General Consumption Tax 
(GCT), GCT Regulations or any other relevant Legislation.   

8 

 
 
 
 
 
 TECHNICAL ADVISORY 
The General Consumption Tax: Treatment of Insurance coverages for marine activities, 
aviation and other related activities carried on at a shipping port and international airport 
in Jamaica. 

•  Outside of a definition accorded in the legislation, the literal meaning of this word is taken. 
Therefore, it is reasonable to accept that in the context of this provision (read provision) 
“to render a service at a port or international airport,” means that the performance of that 
service must take place physically at the port or international airport. This does not apply 
to  the provision  of insurance services where its supply is  made at  the time of  payment, 
which precedes the activities at the port and the insurable risks that may occur. Marine and 
aviation insurance, by nature, are contracted through brokers, insurers, or online platforms, 
and  not  physically  rendered  at  the  port  or  international  airport.  The  place  of  supply  is 
typically considered to be where the service is performed or consumed. In this case, marine 
or aviation insurance is not performed at the port or international airport; it merely relates 
to goods or people that may be at the port or international airport. This distinguishes it from 
services like cargo handling or customs clearance, which are physically performed on site.  

Issue #2: How does one determine that a service is ‘in connection with’ an activity? 

Definition of the term ‘in connection with’ 

The GCT Act does not define the term ‘in connection with’. However, in the case of Real Resorts 
Ltd.  v The Commissioner of General Consumption Tax, a narrow interpretation was given to the 
term where it was the opinion of the courts that for a service to be deemed to be ‘in connection 
with’, “it must sufficiently be closely connected to the taxable activity”.  In other words, the service 
must have a direct, immediate link with the activity. Similarly, in the Commissioners of Taxation 
v Trustees of St. Mark’s Glebe, a narrow interpretation was applied to the term as it was concluded 
that the intent of the section of the statute in question justified the words being given a narrow 
interpretation.  

These principles can be brought to bear in the case of Marine Insurance and Aviation Insurance 
for the purposes of exemption from GCT. Within the context of the activities outlined (i.e. the 
importation or exportation of goods or the transportation of people within and out of Jamaica) 
these types of insurance policies are connected to the importation and exportation of goods and 
the transportation of people into or out of Jamaica. A similar argument can also be made for 
Aviation Liability Insurance. However, there must be a real, substantial, and functional nexus 
with activities at the port   because the service must also be physically rendered at the port.

Issue #3:  Does Marine/Maritime, Aviation or other related insurance services qualify for 
exemption pursuant to the Third Schedule of the GCT Act? 

Is Marine Insurance a service that is rendered at the Port? 

•  Marine  Insurance  is  a  type  of  insurance  that  provides  coverage  against  risks  and  losses 
associated with marine and maritime activities. There are different arms of this insurance 
ranging from coverage that protects risks associated with shipping goods by sea, inland 
waterways  or  air.  It  also  covers  damage  to  vessels,  cargo,  or  liability  for  third  party 
damages.  

•  This  type  of  insurance  is  not  a  service  that  is  typically  rendered  from  a  fixed  place  of 
business  at  the  port.  The  nature  of  the  insurance  is  that  while  some  level  of  insurance-
related  services  may  be  available  at  the  ports  e.g.  through  brokers  or  agents  offering 
information  or  even  selling  this  particular  insurance  itself,  it  is  not  exclusive  to  port 
locations and can be obtained and managed from various other locations. The insurance 
coverage is usually in effect during the entire voyage from the point of departure to the 
destination rather than being provided at and within the designated port(s). It should also 
be noted that the time of supply of the insurance service is when payment is made for it 
and this precedes the eventuality of any risk materializing on the port. 

Is Aviation Liability/Airport Liability Insurance a service rendered at the International 
Airport? 

•  As  outlined  above,  Aviation  Liability  Insurance  is  a  type  of  insurance  coverage  that  is 
provided by insurance companies to protect persons involved in aviation activities, such as 
aircraft  owners,  operators,  pilots,  ground  handling  and  maintenance  providers,  against 
liabilities  arising  from  accidents,  injuries,  or  property  damage.  The  Civil  Aviation  Act 
requires the purchase of an Airport Liability Policy which covers “passengers, aircraft and 
otherwise” for airport operators and airlines to render their services at the airport. 

•  Aviation liability insurance is typically obtained through insurance brokers or companies 
specializing in  aviation  insurance. These insurance providers  assess the risks associated 
with  aviation  activities  and  offer  coverage  options  tailored  to  the  specific  needs  of 
individuals or organizations involved in the aviation industry. These insurance policies are 
usually  purchased  and  managed  outside  of  the  airport  premises,  through  traditional 
insurance  channels.  Therefore,  they  are  not  services  that  fall  within  the  ambit  of  the

by law. 

12) Guidance 

• 

Item 27 of Part II of the Third Schedule limits the exemption to services (except catering 
services) rendered at a port or international airport in Jamaica. There is a clear distinction 
between the service of providing insurance protection against the risks that may materialize 
from conducting marine, maritime and aviation activities at a port or airport or between 
them, respectively; and the actual execution of these activities at the port or international 
airport or between them. These insurance services are not part of the maritime, marine or 
aviation services rendered at the port or international airport.  

•  The purpose for which Item 27 exists is to exempt from GCT certain activities carried out 
at either a port or an international airport. To be rendered at the port, the services must be 
physically performed within the geographic boundaries of the port facility. Therefore, for 
this exemption to apply, the service provider must be physically present and execute the 
service within the boundaries of the port or airport.  

•  However,  these  activities  do  not  include  Marine  or  Aviation  Insurance,  which  is  only 
necessary  for  indemnifying  affected  persons  should  any  loss  or  damage  to  property  or 
persons  occur  from  the  conduct  of  the  exempt  activities  at  the  port  or  airport.  This 
indemnification is  obtained in  advance and is  usually away  from  the ports.  Further, the 
inclusion  of  the  bracketed  phrase  “(excluding  catering  services)”  implies  the  class  of 
persons to enjoy the exemption benefits. This class references persons carrying out day to 
day functions of an operational nature at the ports with respect to trade (import/export) and 
travel (exit/entry into Jamaica) but excluding catering services; the latter although carried 
out at that location does not even qualify for the exemption.  

•  Thus, the arrangement of Marine Insurance and Aviation Insurance that typically occurs 
before the goods, aircraft or ship  arrives at the port cannot be construed as meeting the 
statutory criteria for exemption from GCT because it is not rendered at the port. Merely 
verifying  documentation  of  this  insurance  at  the  port  does  not  amount  to  rendering  the 
insurance service at the port. 

Advisory #: 022026/01/GCT-TA 
DISCLAIMER: This Advisory is a guide only and is not a substitute for the General Consumption Tax

Conclusion 

Guiding Principles on Insurance Policies/Coverages in relation to Marine/Maritime or 
Aviation Liability 

•  Section 6 (7) of the GCT Act prescribes the time of supply for ‘insurance contracts’: that 
is,  when  payment  is  made  to  an  insurer  or  broker.  Unlike  a  policy  of  life  assurance  or 
reinsurance, marine and aviation insurance are not insurance contracts excluded from the 
definition of “contract of insurance" in section 6 (8) of the Act. Nor are they specifically 
exempted  in  Item  13  (which  only  prescribes  life  assurance  services)  or  Item  27  (which 
broadly covers financial services) of Part II of the Third Schedule.      

•  The  principles  articulated  above  are  therefore  applicable  to  similar  /related  insurance 
coverages including, Air Cargo Policy, Airport Liability Policy or any Transport Insurance 
for  services  rendered  at  a  port  or  international  airport  in  relation  to  the  importation  or 
exportation  of  goods  or  the  transportation  of  people  into  and  out  of  Jamaica.  These 
insurance coverages are not considered as being rendered at a port or international airport 
and  consequently  do  not  qualify  for  exemption  under  Item  27  of  Part  II  of  the  Third 
Schedule.

V. 

Case Laws 

▪  Real Resort Limited v Commissioner of General Consumption Tax 

The Jamaican courts had to consider whether or not the appellant was carrying on a taxable 
activity within section 2 (2)(b) of the GCT Act and was therefore entitled to claim input 
tax. Under section 2 (2)(b) of the said Act a taxable activity is defined as “anything done 
in connection with the commencement or termination of that activity”. The court took the 
view  that  unless  an  activity  has  a  direct  or  immediate  link  to  another  activity,  the  first 
cannot be said to be ‘in connection with’ the second.
